[[File:Illustration Tanacetum vulgare0.jpg|thumb|240px|Illustration of a tansy]]

'''Tansy''' ('''''Tanacetum vulgare''''') is a [[perennial]], [[herbaceous]] flowering plant in the genus ''[[Tanacetum]]'' in the family [[Asteraceae]], native to temperate Europe and Asia.<ref name="POWO"/> It has been introduced to other parts of the world, including Australia and North and South America,<ref name="POWO"/> and in some areas has become [[Invasive species|invasive]]. It is also known as '''common tansy''',<ref>{{PLANTS|id=TAVU|taxon=Tanacetum vulgare|access-date=8 December 2015}}</ref> '''bitter buttons''', '''cow bitter''', or '''golden buttons'''.{{citation needed|date=June 2026}} The Latin word ''vulgare'' means "common".<ref name="Stearn">{{cite book |last=Stearn |first=William T. |title=Botanical Latin: history, grammar, syntax, terminology, and vocabulary |publisher=David & Charles |publication-place=Newton Abbot, Devon |date=1983 |isbn=0-7153-8548-8 |page=545}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File: Rainfarn mit Ameisen.jpeg|thumb|220px| Tansy: corymb of flower heads with recognisable [[Fibonacci sequence|Fibonacci]] spirals]]

Tansy is a flowering herbaceous [[clonal colony|clump-forming]] plant with finely divided compound leaves and yellow, button-like flowers. It has a stout, somewhat reddish, erect stem, usually smooth, {{convert|50–150|cm|abbr=on}} tall, and branching near the top. The [[leaf|leaves]] are alternate, {{convert|10–15|cm|abbr=on}} long and are [[pinnate]]ly lobed, divided almost to the midrib into about seven pairs of segments, or lobes, which are again divided into smaller lobes having saw-toothed edges, giving the leaf a somewhat fern-like appearance. The roundish, flat-topped, button-like, yellow [[flower]] heads are produced in terminal clusters from mid-to-late summer, typically July to September in Great Britain; each 'button' flowerhead 7–12 mm diameter.<ref name="Streeter">{{cite book |last1=Streeter |first1=David |last2=Hart-Davies |first2=Christina |title=Collins flower guide: the most complete guide to the flowers of Britain and Europe |publisher=HarperCollins |publication-place=London |date=2009 |isbn=978-0-00-718389-0 |pages=502–503}}</ref><ref name="Blamey">{{cite book |last1=Blamey |first1=Marjorie |last2=Grey-Wilson |first2=C. |title=The Illustrated Flora of Britain and northern Europe |publisher=Hodder & Stoughton |publication-place=London |date=1989 |isbn=0-340-40170-2 |pages=410–411}}</ref> The scent is similar to that of [[camphor]] with hints of [[rosemary]]. The leaves and flowers are toxic if consumed in large quantities; the volatile oil contains toxic compounds including [[thujone]], which can cause convulsions and liver and brain damage. Some insects, notably the [[tansy beetle]] ''Chrysolina graminis'', have resistance to the toxins and subsist almost exclusively on the plant.

==Distribution==
Tansy is native to Eurasia; it is native in almost all parts of Europe, including Great Britain, though introduced in Iceland, Ireland, and Portugal.<ref name="POWO"/> It is absent from [[Siberia]] and from some of the [[Mediterranean]] islands;<ref>{{cite journal|last1= Zohary|first1= D.|last2= Heywood |first2= V.H.|title= A Catalogue of the Wild Relatives of Cultivated Plants Native to Europe|journal= Bocconea|year= 1997|url= http://www.pgrforum.org/Zohary_Heywood_Catalogue.htm}}</ref> in Asia, it is native south to Turkey, Kazakhstan, northern China, Korea, and Japan, but absent further south.<ref name="POWO"/> 

==Cultivation and use==
The ancient Greeks may have been the first to cultivate it as a medicinal herb.<ref name="lecain-ailments">{{cite web | last1= LeCain | first1= Ron | last2= Sheley | first2=Roger |last3=Mangold | first3=Jane  | ref = {{harvid|LeCain|2019}} | title=Common tansy (''Tanacetum vulgare'') | year= 2019 | url= https://store.msuextension.org/publications/AgandNaturalResources/MT199911AG.pdf |access-date= 2022-06-23 | page = 2 | quote = The first historical records of common tansy cultivation are from the ancient Greeks who used it for a variety of ailments.}}</ref> In the sixteenth century it was considered to be "necessary for a garden" in England.<ref>{{cite book|last= Harvey |first=John H. | year = 1989 |title= Garden plants of around 1525: the Fromond list|pages=122–134 | edition = reprint | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=LLwhNQEACAAJ}}</ref>

===History of use===
Tansy has a long history of use. The first historical records of its cultivation [[medicinal plant |for medicinal purposes]] involved the ancient [[Greeks]].<ref name="lecain-ailments"/> In the 8th century AD it was grown in the [[herb garden]]s of [[Charlemagne]] and by [[Benedictine]] monks of the Swiss monastery of [[Saint Gall]].{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}} Tansy was used to treat intestinal worms, [[rheumatism]], digestive problems, fevers, sores, and to bring out [[measles]].{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}}<ref name=lestrange>{{cite book|last= LeStrange|first=Richard |title=A History of Herbal Plants  |publisher=[[Angus & Robertson]]|location= London|year= 1977|isbn= 978-0-207-95645-4}}</ref><ref name=mitich>{{cite journal|last=Mitich  |first=Larry W.|title=Tansy|journal=Weed Technology |volume= 6|pages=242–244|date=March 1992|issue=1 |doi=10.1017/S0890037X00034643|bibcode=1992WeedT...6..242M |s2cid=251577774 }}</ref><ref name=zimdahl>{{cite book|last= Zimdahl |first= Richard|title= Weeds and Words|publisher= [[Iowa State University]] Press|location= Ames|year= 1989|isbn= 978-0-8138-0128-5|url=https://archive.org/details/weedswordsety00zimd}}</ref><ref name=durant>{{cite book|last= Durant|first= Mary|title= Who Named the Daisy? Who Named the Rose? |publisher=[[Dodd, Mead and Company]]|location=New York|year=1976}}</ref>

During the [[Middle Ages]] and later, high doses were used to induce [[abortion]]s.<ref name=mitich/><ref name=kingsbury>{{cite book|last= Kingsbury|first= John Merriam|title= Poisonous Plants of the United States and Canada|publisher= [[Prentice-Hall]]|location=Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey|year=1964|isbn=978-0-13-685016-8|url= https://archive.org/details/poisonousplantso00king}}</ref><ref name=illinois>{{cite web|title=Illinois Wildflowers  |url= http://www.illinoiswildflowers.info/weeds/plants/cm_tansy_cr.htm|access-date= 2008-12-16}}</ref> On the other hand, tansy was also used to help women conceive and to prevent miscarriages.<ref name=lestrange/><ref name=mitich/><ref name=haughton>{{cite book |last=Haughton|first=Claire Shaver|title=Green Immigrants |publisher=[[Harcourt Brace]]|location=New York|year= 1980|isbn= 978-0-15-636492-8}}</ref> In the 15th century, Christians began serving tansy with [[Lent]]en meals to commemorate the Passover [[maror| bitter herbs]] eaten by the Israelites.<ref name=durant/><ref name=haughton/> Tansy was thought to have the added Lenten benefits of controlling flatulence brought on by days of eating fish and [[Legume |pulses]]<ref name=lestrange/><ref name=mitich/> and of preventing the intestinal worms believed to be caused by eating fish during Lent.<ref name=sumner/>

Tansy was used as a face wash and was reported to lighten and purify the skin.<ref name=lestrange/><ref name=mitich/> In the 19th century, [[Ireland |Irish]] folklore suggested that bathing in a solution of tansy and salts would cure joint pain.<ref name=egan/>

==Insect repellent==
Tansy has also been used as [[insect repellent]]{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}} and in embalming.<ref name=mitich/><ref name=zimdahl/> It was packed into coffins, wrapped in funeral winding sheets, and tansy [[wreath]]s were sometimes placed on the dead.{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}}<ref name=mitich/><ref name=zimdahl/><ref name=haughton/> [[Henry Dunster]], the first president of [[Harvard University]], was buried wearing a tansy wreath in a coffin packed with tansy; when the cemetery was moved in 1846 the tansy had maintained its shape and fragrance, helping to identify the president's remains.{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}}<ref name=mitich/><ref name=haughton/> By the 19th century, tansy was used so much at New England funerals that people began to disdain it for its morbid association with death.<ref name=mitich/><ref name=durant/>

During the American colonial period, meat was frequently rubbed with or packed in tansy leaves to repel insects and delay spoilage.{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}}<ref name=mitich/><ref name=haughton/> Tansy was frequently worn at that time in shoes to prevent [[malaria]] and other [[fever]]s;<ref name=mitich/><ref name=haughton/> it has been shown, however, that some mosquito species, including ''[[Culex pipiens]]'', take nectar from tansy flowers.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1365-2915.1987.tb00323.x |author1=Andersson, I.H. |author2= Jaeson, T.G.T.  |title=Nectar feeding by mosquitoes in Sweden, with special reference to ''Culex pipiens'' and ''Cx. torrentium'' |journal=Medical and Veterinary Entomology |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=59–64 |year=1987 |pmid=2979521|s2cid=30469080 }}</ref>

Tansy can be used as in [[companion planting]] and for [[biological pest control]]. It is planted alongside potatoes to repel the [[Colorado potato beetle]], with one study finding tansy reduced the beetle population by 60 to 100 percent.<ref name=mitich/><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/np50036a009 |author=Schearer, W.R. |title=Components of oil of tansy (''Tanacetum vulgare'') that repel Colorado potato beetle (''Leptinotarsa decemlineata'') |journal=Journal of Natural Products |volume=47 |issue=6 |pages=964–9 |year=1984 |bibcode=1984JNAtP..47..964S }}</ref>{{sfn|LeCain|2019|p=2}}

In England tansy is placed on window sills to repel flies; sprigs are placed in bed linen to drive away pests, and it has been used as an ant repellent.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Drury, S.|title=Plants and Pest Control in England circa 1400–1700: A Preliminary Study |journal=Folklore|volume=103|pages=103–6|year=1992|doi=10.1080/0015587x.1992.9715833}}</ref>

In the 1940s, distilled tansy oil mixed with [[fleabane]], [[Mentha pulegium|pennyroyal]] and diluted alcohol was a well-known [[mosquito repellent]]; collectors were paid five cents a pound for tansy in full bloom.<ref name=mitich/><ref>{{cite book |author=Georgia, A.E. |title=A Manual of Weeds  |publisher=MacMillan |location=New York |year=1942}}</ref> Research has found that tansy extracts do indeed repel mosquitoes, but not as effectively as products containing [[DEET]].<ref name=mitich/><ref name=DePooter89>{{cite journal |author1=DePooter, H.L. |author2= Vermeesch, J. |author3= Schamp, N.M. |journal=Journal of Essential Oil Research|title=unk|volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=9–13 |year=1989}}</ref> In 2008, researchers in Sweden investigated the use of tansy to repel ticks, showing a 64–72 percent repellency for each oil constituent.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1603/0022-2585(2008)45[88:TRSITE]2.0.CO;2 |vauthors=Pålsson K, Jaenson TG, Baeckström P, Borg-Karlson AK |title=Tick repellent substances in the essential oil of ''Tanacetum vulgare'' |journal=Journal of Medical Entomology |volume=45 |issue=1 |pages=88–93 |date=January 2008 |doi-broken-date=12 January 2026 |pmid=18283947|s2cid=24970966 }}</ref>

==Toxicity==
[[File:Close up of Tanacetum vulgare flower head.JPG|thumb|200px|Detail of Tansy inflorescences]]
Many tansy species contain a volatile oil which can cause [[contact dermatitis]] in sensitive individuals. If taken internally, toxic metabolites are produced as the oil is broken down in the liver and digestive tract. It is highly toxic to internal parasites, and for centuries tansy tea has been prescribed by herbalists to [[Anthelmintic|expel worms]]. Tansy is an effective insecticide and is highly toxic to [[arthropod]]s.<ref>Edible and Medicinal Plants of the West, Gregory L. Tilford, {{ISBN|0-87842-359-1}}</ref> Because it contains [[thujone]], the U.S. [[Food and Drug Administration (United States)|FDA]] limits the use of tansy to alcoholic beverages, and the final product must be thujone-free.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20030915173705/http://www.accessdata.fda.gov/scripts/cdrh/cfdocs/cfcfr/CFRSearch.cfm?FR=172.510 Food Additives Permitted for Direct Addition to Food for Human Consumption.] Food and Drug Administration (2007). Retrieved 30 Mar 2008.</ref> Blue tansy (''[[Vogtia annua]]'', syn. ''Tanacetum annuum'') is often confused with common tansy (''Tanacetum vulgare'') but the former produces an essential oil that is completely different chemically as it contains no thujone and high amounts of [[chamazulene]] making the oil dark blue in colour, giving rise to its common name of Blue Tansy Oil.<ref>J. Essent. Oil Res., Vol. 11, 343-348 (1999)</ref><ref>J. Essent. Oil Res., Vol. 12, 122-124 (Jan/Feb 2000)</ref> Despite claims by some unethical resellers of essential oils who adulterate the very expensive blue tansy oil with the much cheaper oil from ''Tanacetum vulgare'', the oil from ''Tanacetum vulgare'' is never blue in colour as it contains no chamazulene.<ref>J. Agric. Food Chem., 2004, 52 (6), pp 1742–1748</ref><ref>J. Nat. Prod., 1984, 47 (6), pp 964–969.</ref> For this reason a high thujone oil from ''Tanacetum vulgare'' should never be referred to as "Blue Tansy" oil and any such blue oil containing significant thujone is an adulterated product.

The active components of the volatile oil include [[eucalyptol|1,8-cineole]], ''trans''-[[thujone]], [[camphor]] and [[Myrica gale|myrtenol]], with the quantities and proportions of each varying seasonally and from plant to plant.<ref name=mitich/><ref name=DePooter89/><ref name=Jacobs08>{{cite web |author=Jacobs, J. |title=Ecological Management of Common Tansy (''Tanacetum vulgare'' L.) |website=Invasive Species Technical Note # MT-18 |publisher=United States Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service |url=http://www.msuextension.org/ruralliving/Dream/PDF/ctansy.pdf |date=February 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110718202020/http://www.msuextension.org/ruralliving/Dream/PDF/ctansy.pdf |archive-date=18 July 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=Judzentiene05>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/j.bse.2004.11.003 |author1=Judzentiene, A. | author2=Mockute, D. |title=The inflorescence and leaf essential oils of ''Tanacetum vulgare'' L. var. vulgare growing wild in Lithuania |journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology |volume=33 |issue=5 |pages=487–498 |year=2005|bibcode=2005BioSE..33..487J }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/S0305-1978(00)00056-9 |author1=Keskitalo, M. | author2= Pehu E. |author3= Simon, J.E. |title=Variation in volatile compounds from tansy (''Tanacetum vulgare'' L.) related to genetic and morphological differenced of genotypes |journal=Biochemical Systematics and Ecology |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=267–285 |year=2001 |pmid=11152946|bibcode=2001BioSE..29..267K }}</ref>

1,8-Cineole is a toxin believed to defend the plant leaves against attacks by herbivores.<ref name=Jacobs08/><ref name=Judzentiene05/>

==Culinary uses==

[[File:Tanacetum vulgare blatt.jpeg|thumb|Tansy foil]]

Tansy was formerly used as a flavouring for [[pudding]]s and [[omelette]]s, but is now almost unknown, except in [[Cork (city)|Cork]], where it is used in a sauce to accompany [[drisheen]]s. The herbalist [[John Gerard]] (c. 1545–1612) noted that tansy was well known as "pleasant in taste", and he recommends tansy sweetmeats as "an especial thing against the gout, if every day for a certain space a reasonable quantitie thereof be eaten fasting." In [[Yorkshire]], tansy and [[caraway]] seeds were traditionally used in biscuits served at funerals.<ref name=sumner />

During the [[Stuart Restoration]] in the late 1600s, a "tansy" was a sweet omelette flavoured with tansy juice. In the BBC documentary "[[The Supersizers...|The Supersizers go ... Restoration]]", [[Allegra McEvedy]] described the flavour as "fruity, sharpness to it and then there's a sort of explosion of cool heat a bit like peppermint."<ref>//www.youtube.com/watch?v=TCfx98Ei5lM and //www.youtube.com/watch?v=fCiBMDhs5p0</ref> However, [[Sue Perkins]], the programme's presenter, experienced tansy toxicity.

According to liquor historian A. J. Baime, in the 19th century [[Tennessee]] [[whisky|whiskey]] magnate [[Jack Daniel]] enjoyed drinking his own whiskey with [[sugar]] and crushed tansy leaf.

[[File:Tansies in MI,UP.jpg|thumb|upright|The flowers are naturally "petal-less".]]

In the [[Belgium|Belgian]] coastal province of [[West Flanders]] small quantities of crushed dried tansy leaf were traditionally used as culinary herb to spice up [[pancake]]s and [[omelette]]s. There tansy is colloquially known as ''pannenkoekenkruid'' ("pancake herb").

It can also be used as a substitute for [[salvia officinalis|sage.]]<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-year=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=407}}</ref>

==Ethnomedical use==

For many years, tansy has been used as a [[herbalism|medicinal herb]] despite its toxicity. 19th-century [[Ireland|Irish]] folklore suggests bathing in a solution of tansy and salt as a cure for joint pain.<ref name="egan">{{cite journal |last=Egan |first=F.A. |title=Irish Folk-Lore. Medical Plants |journal=The Folk-Lore Journal |volume=5 |issue=1 |pages=11–13 |year=1887|doi=10.1080/17442524.1887.10602835 }}</ref> A bitter tea made with tansy flowers has been used for centuries as an [[anthelmintic]] to treat parasitic worm infestations, and tansy cakes were traditionally eaten during [[Lent]] because it was believed that eating fish during Lent caused intestinal worms.<ref name="sumner">{{cite book |author=Sumner, Judith |title=American Household Botany: A History of Useful Plants, 1620–1900 |publisher=Timber Press |location=Portland, Or |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-88192-652-1}}</ref> Various ''Tanacetum'' species are used [[ethnomedicine|ethnomedically]] to treat [[migraine]], [[neuralgia]] and [[rheumatism]] and as anthelmintics. Traditionally, tansy was often used for its [[emmenagogue]] effects to bring on menstruation or end an unwanted pregnancy, and pregnant women are advised to not use this herb.<ref name=arnold>{{cite book |last=Martin |first=Corinne |title=Herbal Remedies from the Wild |publisher=The Countryman Press |year=2000  |location=Woodstock, Vermont |pages=133–135 |isbn=978-0-88150-485-9}}</ref>

===Among Native Americans===

The [[Cherokee]] use an [[infusion]] of the plant for backache, use the plant as a [[Herbal tonic|tonic]], and wear it around the waist and in shoes to prevent miscarriages.<ref>Hamel, Paul B. and Mary U. Chiltoskey 1975 Cherokee Plants and Their Uses -- A 400 Year History. Sylva, N.C. Herald Publishing Co. (p. 58)</ref> The [[Cheyenne]] use an infusion of the pulverised leaves and blossoms for dizziness and weakness.<ref>Grinnell, George Bird 1972 ''The Cheyenne Indians - Their History and Ways of Life'' Vol.2. Lincoln. University of Nebraska Press (p. 190).</ref>

==Other uses==

[[File:Tanacetum vulgare 20041012 2570.jpg|thumb|upright|Tansy]]

Some traditional dyers use tansy to produce a golden-yellow colour.<ref>{{cite web|last=Suomi|first=Päivi|title=A Dyer's Walk|year=2001|url=http://www.allfiberarts.com/library/dyeplants/bltansy.htm|access-date=2007-05-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929063355/http://www.allfiberarts.com/library/dyeplants/bltansy.htm|archive-date=2007-09-29|url-status=dead}}</ref> The yellow flowers are dried for use in floral arrangements.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

Tansy is also used as a [[companion plant]], especially with [[Cucurbitaceae|cucurbits]] like [[cucumbers]] and [[Squash (plant)|squash]], or with [[rose]]s or berries. It is thought to repel insects.{{cn|date=August 2026}}

Dried tansy is used by some [[beekeeper]]s as fuel in a [[bee smoker]].{{cn|date=August 2026}}
